papers.title: From consensus to evidence: Bridging the gap in pharmacotherapy for insomnia and sleep dysfunction in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: This letter commends the Parkinson Study Group for their comprehensive consensus on sleep in Parkinson's disease while addressing critical gaps in insomnia and depression management. It emphasizes the need for evidence-based pharmacotherapies, avoiding off-label sedating antidepressants, and prioritizing rigorously designed clinical trials for non-motor sleep disturbances.

Neuroinflammation in levodopa-induced dyskinesia in Parkinson's disease: current state of the art.
papers.abstract: Levodopa-induced dyskinesia (LID) remains a major limitation of long-term dopaminergic therapy in Parkinson's disease (PD). Although LID is classically attributed to maladaptive corticostriatal plasticity driven by pulsatile dopaminergic stimulation in the dopamine-denervated striatum, accumulating evidence indicates that chronic neuroinflammation may lower the threshold for LID development and expression. Here, we synthesize preclinical, human biomarkers, neuroimaging, and genetic findings that support neuroinflammation as a mechanistic bridge between cellular stress and circuit-level maladaptation. In animal models, pharmacological modulation of inflammation-linked pathways, particularly nitrergic signaling, antibiotic repurposing, and cannabinoid-based strategies, attenuates abnormal involuntary movements and reduces striatal glial reactivity, implicating an inflammation-plasticity coupling in LID. In humans, post-mortem studies implicate regionally constrained mitochondrial DNA abnormalities and lipid dysregulation in the striatum, while biofluid metabolomics supports altered nitric oxide generation and lipid pathways associated with LID severity. Neuroimaging studies reveal markers consistent with oxidative stress and neurovascular dysfunction, and genetic studies link LID risk to variants in genes involved in lysosomal function, mitochondrial homeostasis, and inflammatory transcriptional programs. Integrated with the classic mechanisms of LID pathophysiology, we propose a conceptual model organized around three interrelated dimensions: (i) the topographical distribution of neuroinflammatory changes, particularly within the striatum; (ii) the interaction of neuroinflammation with mitochondrial dysfunction and lipid dysregulation; and (iii) the modifying influence of genetic susceptibility. This model motivates biomarker-guided, randomized trials targeting specific inflammatory nodes to prevent or mitigate LID.

papers.title: Stage-Dependent Sarcopenia Status in Parkinson's Disease: An ICF-Based ISarcoPRM Algorithm.
papers.journal: American journal of physical medicine & rehabilitation
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to determine sarcopenia status in patients with Parkinson's disease (PD), classified as early-stage (<2.5) and moderate-stage (≥2.5) by the Modified Hoehn and Yahr Scale, and in healthy controls using the ICF-based ISarcoPRM algorithm. DESIGN: A total of 63 participants were included in this cross-sectional study: 42 patients with PD and 21 healthy controls. Muscle mass was assessed using ultrasonographic anterior thigh thickness (ATT) and the Sonographic Thigh Adjustment Ratio (STAR), muscle strength by handgrip dynamometry, and physical performance by the five-times sit-to-stand test (5xSTS). Participants were classified as non-sarcopenic, dynapenic, or sarcopenic according to ISarcoPRM criteria. RESULTS: The prevalence of sarcopenia differed significantly across groups (P=0.016), with higher rates observed in patients with moderate-stage PD. Adjusted analyses showed significant overall group differences in ATT, handgrip strength, STAR, and 5xSTS performance, with muscle-related impairments generally more pronounced in the moderate-stage PD group. No significant differences were found between early-stage PD and healthy controls. CONCLUSION: Muscle-related impairments in PD appear to be stage-dependent and become more pronounced in moderate stages. Comprehensive assessment approaches integrating muscle morphology, strength, and physical performance may provide clinically relevant insights for individualized rehabilitation strategies.
